page: Amazon Web Services r8g.medium is a memory-optimized virtual machine instance powered by an AWS Graviton Neoverse-V2 processor. Operating on the arm64 architecture, this instance features 1 dedicated physical core with 1 thread, running at a clock speed of 2.8 GHz. It is equipped with 8.0 GB of system memory, providing a high memory-to-vCPU ratio of 8 GB per core. The processor includes 64 KB of L1d cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 36 MB of L3 cache, with hardware support for AES cryptographic acceleration. This instance does not include local storage or GPU accelerators, and operates on the AWS Nitro hypervisor with a baseline network bandwidth of 1 Gbps.

Benchmark data reveals a clear distinction between single-core and multi-core performance profiles. The single-core capabilities of the Neoverse-V2 processor are moderate, with stress-ng single-core CPU performance, Geekbench single-core, and single-threaded gzip compression scoring in the average range. Single-threaded bzip3 decompression demonstrates strong performance. However, due to the single-core limitation of this specific instance size, multi-core benchmarks such as stress-ng multi-core, Geekbench multi-core, and software compilation with Clang fall into the poor category. Memory bandwidth tests also show lower throughput, with large-block write speeds at 11.94 GB/sec and small-block cached reads at 115.67 GB/sec.

The r8g.medium offers a cost-efficient entry point into the memory-optimized Graviton8 family, delivering a high memory allocation relative to its single vCPU without the overhead of multi-threaded resource contention. The primary tradeoff is the strict single-core limitation, which restricts its utility for parallel processing, heavy database operations, or high-throughput web serving, as evidenced by weak Passmark database scores and poor static web serving throughput. This instance is best suited for lightweight, memory-bound workloads that do not require multi-threaded execution, such as small-scale caching layers, single-threaded background workers, low-traffic memory-resident applications, or basic development and testing environments.
